newsitem.title: UK: Britain's new fraudbusting head faces tough task.
newsitem.headline: Britain's new fraudbusting head faces tough task.

text.p: Britain's Serious Fraud Office (SFO), better known for its failures than successes, on Monday got a new director in the form of lawyer Rosalind Wright.

Wright succeeds George Staple next month following her appointment by Attorney General Sir Nicholas Lyell. At the time of her appointment, she was general counsel and an executive director at financial watchdog the Securities and Futures Authority.
Staple, who has been SFO head for the past five years, is due to return to private practice. He is a partner at law firm Clifford Chance and is expected to resume his role there.
Wright will be the fourth SFO director and the second woman to have run the office. The SFO said she was a "very experienced prosecutor and City regulator" and welcomed her appointment.
She was head of the fraud investigation group in the Director of Public Prosecution's department between 1983 and 1987.

The SFO, which investigates and prosecutes Britain's most serious and complex fraud cases, was set up in 1988 with the aim of bringing more of these complicated white-collar crimes to trial and putting the perpetrators behind bars.
But the office has fought an uphill battle against unfavourable public and media opinion following several high-profile acquittals and perceived "failures" to get convictions.
These have included the acquittal of former boxer George Walker in 1994 for an alleged 164 million pound ($262 million) fraud on creditors and shareholders in his leisure group Brent Walker.

The acquittal of Kevin and Ian Maxwell almost a year ago on fraud charges and the subsequent throwing out of a second trial against Kevin, son of the late tycoon Robert Maxwell, were also widely viewed as blows.
Staple has defended the office, saying it was wrong to judge it merely on a number of notable acquittals. The SFO says it has an overall conviction rate of around 63 percent.

The SFO has managed to achieve notable convictions. It secured the conviction of Peter Clowes in the Barlow Clowes financial scandal as well as getting results in all of the Bank of Credit and Commerce International (BCCI) cases it has brought to trial. It said that more than three out of four cases has ended in at least one conviction. Of 154 cases brought to trial since its inception, 219 out of a total of 349 defendants have been convicted.
Senior lawyers have said the SFO was being used as a scapegoat for shortcomings in the British legal system's ability to deal with complex frauds.
This has led to calls for a revision to the jury system in crimes involving complicated investments, with suggestions that a specialist panel may be more appropriate than a lay jury.
After the throwing out of the second Maxwell case, Staple himself said the ruling weakened the system of trying people accused of major financial fraud.

He described the system as emasculated because the ruling meant that later severed indictments, where charges are split up to produce a series of manageable trials, were unlikely to be pursued after an acquittal.

Staple also questioned whether it was reasonable to ask a lay jury to sit through an entire lengthy case and at the end of the process deliver a verdict. He said a solution to the problems raised was urgently needed.
Other questions still facing the SFO, which the incoming Wright will have to overcome, are the huge cost of such trials and Britain's ability to prosecute international fraud.

Among the cases it is currently considering for investigation is that of Peter Young, the Morgan Grenfell Asset Management fund manager sacked last year by parent bank Deutsche Morgan Grenfell after the discovery of irregularities in three of its funds. ($ = 0.625 British Pounds)
